summary.text: Reflection under \(k\mapsto n-k\), together with \(\binom{p+d}{k}\equiv\binom d k+\binom d{k-p}\pmod p\) and the corresponding central-binomial divisibility, makes every Hankel entry beyond the anti-diagonal vanish modulo \(p\), while the anti-diagonal values are \(1\) and \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), respectively. Reversing the columns makes each matrix triangular, so the reversal sign \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\) and the powers of those anti-diagonal values give the two claimed residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                    \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and write
\[
p=2h+1,\qquad h=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All congruences below are modulo \(p\), or equivalently identities in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We first establish the binomial congruences that will be used.

### 1. Basic binomial congruences

In \(\mathbb F_p[X]\), the freshman’s dream gives
\[
(1+X)^p=1+X^p.
\]
Consequently, for all nonnegative integers \(d,k\), comparison of the coefficient of \(X^k\) in
\[
(1+X)^{p+d}=(1+X^p)(1+X)^d
\]
gives
\[
\binom{p+d}{k}\equiv
\binom dk+\begin{cases}
\binom d{k-p},&k\ge p,\\
0,&k<p.
\end{cases}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
Here, as usual, \(\binom dr=0\) when \(r>d\).

We will also need two consequences concerning central binomial coefficients. If \(0\le m<p\), then
\[
\binom{2(p+m)}{p+m}\equiv 2\binom{2m}{m}.                     \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, apply (1), first with the upper index written as
\[
2(p+m)=p+(p+2m).
\]
For the coefficient with lower index \(p+m\), this gives
\[
\binom{2(p+m)}{p+m}
\equiv \binom{p+2m}{p+m}+\binom{p+2m}{m}.
\]
The two binomial coefficients on the right are equal by symmetry. Since \(m<p\), a second application of (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+2m}{m}\equiv\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
This proves (2).

If, in addition, \(p\le 2m\), then
\[
\binom{2m}{m}\equiv0.                                        \tag{3}
\]
To see this, note that \(m<p\) and \(2m<2p\). Thus the numerator of
\[
\binom{2m}{m}=\frac{(2m)!}{(m!)^2}
\]
contains exactly one multiple of \(p\), whereas neither denominator factor contains a multiple of \(p\). Hence \(p\mid\binom{2m}{m}\).

Finally, for \(0\le k\le p-1\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k.                                  \tag{4}
\]
For example, for \(k>0\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}
 =\prod_{r=1}^k\frac{p-r}{r}
 \equiv\prod_{r=1}^k\frac{-r}{r}=(-1)^k,
\]
and every \(r\le k<p\) is invertible modulo \(p\). The case \(k=0\) is immediate.

### 2. Odd-indexed terms vanish identically

For every odd nonnegative integer \(n\),
\[
a(n)=0\quad\text{and}\quad c(n)=0                            \tag{5}
\]
as exact integer equalities.

For \(a(n)\), pair the summand indexed by \(k\) with the summand indexed by \(n-k\). Binomial symmetry gives
\[
\binom n{n-k}=\binom nk,
\]
and, because \(n\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{n-k}=-(-1)^k.
\]
Thus the two paired summands are negatives of one another.

For \(c(n)\), the substitution \(k\mapsto n-k\) again leaves \(\binom nk^2\) unchanged and interchanges the two central binomial factors
\[
\binom{2k}{k},\qquad \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Their product is therefore unchanged, while the sign is negated because \(n\) is odd. Again all terms cancel in pairs. Since an odd \(n\) has no fixed point under \(k\mapsto n-k\), this proves (5).

### 3. Vanishing of \(a(p+d)\) for odd \(d<p\)

Let \(d\) be odd with \(0\le d<p\). We claim
\[
a(p+d)\equiv0.                                                \tag{6}
\]
Split the defining sum into the ranges
\[
0\le k<p\quad\text{and}\quad p\le k\le p+d.
\]
In the first range, (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+d}{k}\equiv\binom dk.
\]
If \(k>d\), this is zero. Hence only \(k=x\), \(0\le x\le d\), can contribute from this range, and its contribution is
\[
(-1)^x\binom dx^4.
\]

In the second range write \(k=p+x\), where \(0\le x\le d\). Formula (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+d}{p+x}\equiv\binom dx,
\]
because \(\binom d{p+x}=0\). Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x.
\]
Thus the term indexed by \(p+x\) is
\[
-(-1)^x\binom dx^4,
\]
which cancels the term indexed by \(x\). Summing over \(x=0,\dots,d\) proves (6).

### 4. Vanishing of \(c(p+d)\) for odd \(d<p\)

Under the same assumptions on \(d\), we likewise claim
\[
c(p+d)\equiv0.                                                \tag{7}
\]
Again split the sum at \(p\).

For \(0\le k<p\), (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+d}{k}\equiv\binom dk,
\]
so terms with \(k>d\) vanish. Put \(k=x\) with \(0\le x\le d\), and abbreviate
\[
B_m=\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
The complementary index is
\[
p+d-x=p+(d-x).
\]
Since \(0\le d-x<p\), (2) gives
\[
\binom{2(p+d-x)}{p+d-x}\equiv2B_{d-x}.
\]
Therefore the term indexed by \(x\) is congruent to
\[
2(-1)^x\binom dx^2 B_xB_{d-x}.                                \tag{8}
\]

Now take an index in the second range, writing it as \(k=p+x\), with \(0\le x\le d\). By (1),
\[
\binom{p+d}{p+x}\equiv\binom dx.
\]
By (2),
\[
\binom{2(p+x)}{p+x}\equiv2B_x.
\]
The complementary index is now simply
\[
(p+d)-(p+x)=d-x,
\]
so its central binomial factor is \(B_{d-x}\). Finally,
\[
(-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x.
\]
Thus the term indexed by \(p+x\) is congruent to
\[
-2(-1)^x\binom dx^2B_xB_{d-x},
\]
the negative of (8). The terms cancel pairwise, proving (7).

### 5. All entries in the upper Hankel band vanish

We now show that for either sequence \(s=a\) or \(s=c\),
\[
s(n)\equiv0\qquad(p\le n\le2p-2).                            \tag{9}
\]
If \(n\) is odd, this follows from the exact cancellation (5). If \(n\) is even, write
\[
n=p+d.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(d=n-p\) is odd. Also, from \(p\le n\le2p-2\),
\[
0\le d\le p-2<p.
\]
Thus (6) applies for \(a\), and (7) applies for \(c\). This proves (9) for both sequences.

### 6. Evaluation at the boundary index \(p-1\)

For the first sequence, (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are \(p=2h+1\) terms in this alternating sum, beginning and ending with \(+1\), so
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1.                                                \tag{10}
\]

For the second sequence we prove
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^h.                                          \tag{11}
\]
Since \(p-1=2h\), its \(k\)-th summand contains the central factors
\[
\binom{2k}{k}\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{2(2h-k)}{2h-k}.
\]
We show that every term except \(k=h\) vanishes modulo \(p\).

If \(k>h\), then \(k<p\) and
\[
p=2h+1\le2k.
\]
Thus (3), with \(m=k\), says \(\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0\).

If \(k<h\), put \(m=2h-k=p-1-k\). Then \(m<p\), and
\[
2m=4h-2k\ge2h+2>p,
\]
so (3) gives
\[
\binom{2(2h-k)}{2h-k}=\binom{2m}{m}\equiv0.
\]
Hence only the middle term \(k=h\) remains.

At \(k=h\), all relevant binomial coefficients are \(\binom{2h}{h}=\binom{p-1}{h}\). More precisely, the factor \(\binom{p-1}{h}\) occurs squared, and each of the two central binomial factors is also \(\binom{2h}{h}\). By (4),
\[
\binom{2h}{h}=\binom{p-1}{h}\equiv(-1)^h.
\]
Therefore the middle summand is
\[
(-1)^h\bigl((-1)^h\bigr)^2(-1)^h(-1)^h
=(-1)^{5h}=(-1)^h.
\]
This proves (11).

### 7. A Hankel determinant lemma

We now isolate the determinant argument. Let \(s(0),s(1),\dots\) be elements of \(\mathbb F_p\), and suppose
\[
s(n)=0\quad\text{for }p\le n\le2p-2,
\qquad s(p-1)=v.                                               \tag{12}
\]
Form the \(p\times p\) Hankel matrix
\[
M=(s(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Then
\[
\det M=(-1)^h v^p.                                            \tag{13}
\]

To prove this, reverse the order of the columns. The resulting matrix \(R\) has entries
\[
R_{ij}=s\bigl(i+(p-1-j)\bigr).
\]
If \(j<i\), then
\[
p\le i+p-1-j\le2p-2,
\]
so (12) implies \(R_{ij}=0\). Thus \(R\) is upper triangular. Its diagonal entries are all
\[
R_{ii}=s(p-1)=v.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\det R=v^p.                                                    \tag{14}
\]

The reversal permutation on \(p\) objects has one inversion for every pair of distinct positions, hence has
\[
\binom p2=\frac{p(p-1)}2=ph
\]
inversions. Since \(p\) is odd, \(ph\) has the same parity as \(h\), so the sign of the reversal is \((-1)^h\). Reversing the columns multiplies a determinant by this sign. Therefore
\[
v^p=\det R=(-1)^h\det M.
\]
Since \((-1)^h\) is its own inverse, (13) follows.

### 8. The determinant for \(a(n)\)

Reduce the integer matrix
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\]
entrywise modulo \(p\). Determinants are polynomial expressions with integer coefficients in the matrix entries, so reducing the entries and then taking the determinant gives the reduction of \(\det A\).

By (9), the reduced sequence satisfies the upper-band vanishing condition (12), and by (10) its boundary value is \(v=1\). Applying (13),
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^h1^p=(-1)^h
=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]
This is the first asserted congruence.

### 9. The determinant for \(c(n)\)

Likewise, reduce
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\]
modulo \(p\). The upper-band values vanish by (9), while (11) gives the boundary value
\[
v=(-1)^h.
\]
Formula (13) therefore yields
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^h\bigl((-1)^h\bigr)^p.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd,
\[
\bigl((-1)^h\bigr)^p=(-1)^{hp}=(-1)^h.
\]
Hence
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^h(-1)^h=(-1)^{2h}=1\pmod p.
\]

Thus, for every odd prime \(p\),
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p}.
\]
